 View Comments Miles Teller in “Paper Tiger.” NEON Never go into business with family. That helpful adage is the black heart beating inside writer-director James Gray’s “Paper Tiger.” The movie, which was the opening night film at the 2026 New York Film Festival, marks Gray’s return to his earlier, gangster-driven neo-noir features like “Little Odessa” and “We Own the Night.” This period piece, set in 1986 New York City, benefits from its carefully crafted tension and a surprisingly good performance from Miles Teller. 
 Teller plays Irwin, the nebbishy, bespectacled patriarch of the Pearl family. His wife Linda (Scarlett Johansson) and their two kids, younger son Benjamin (Roman Engel) and older son Scott (Gavin Goudey), live in a modest home in Queens. The Pearls are spending their last few weeks together as a family — Scott is heading off to college soon — and all appears to be well. 
 Irwin believes that the neighborhood is insulated from the crime that New York City was known for at the time. He and Linda are pretty cocky about their lives and their stature; Irwin is a prideful man when it comes to his position in life.

Enter Email Sign Up Miles Teller, left, and Adam Driver in “Paper Tiger.” NEON As the Good Book tells us, “pride goeth before destruction, and a haughty spirit before the fall.” And the fall is a long way down for Irwin Pearl. 
 Enter Gary (Adam Driver), Irwin’s estranged brother. A former cop, Gary is now a very successful businessman. It’s been a while since he and Irwin connected, but Gary still maintains his “cool uncle” status with his nephews. They ask to see Gary’s gun and gaze at him with the wide-eyed wonder that teenage boys have in abundance at that age. 
 Gary has a proposition for his brother, a consulting collaboration between his NYC cop street smarts and Irwin’s work knowledge of city regulations surrounding construction. The job sounds simple enough: pitch their services to businesses working on projects involving the Gowanus Canal. In 1986, there were numerous construction gigs popping up around the notoriously polluted body of water in Brooklyn. Gary pitches the business as a means to elevate his brother’s status. 
 Still from “Paper Tiger.” NEON Or so Irwin thinks. “Paper Tiger” posits that you should never trust anyone who comes to your house with gifts of Peter Luger steaks. Especially if they’ve brought Peter Luger employees to serve them. Irwin’s naivete makes him a trusting soul, a do-gooder who is out of his league in Gary’s world of vipers. 
 Once Gary and Irwin make a deal with some shady Russian businessmen, dollar signs light up in Irwin’s eyes. To score points with Benjamin and Scott, he takes them on a late night visit to the site. There, he sees something he should not have seen. Immediately, Irwin’s family is in extreme danger. From here, Gray ratchets up the tension until the audience is on the edge of their seats. 
 Scarlett Johansson in “Paper Tiger.” NEON While the crime plot takes center stage, a subplot involving Linda gives “Paper Tiger” some emotional weight. Linda receives a troubling medical diagnosis, one she hides from the family. Her dilemma is a counterpoint to the home invasions, threats, and violence that propel the crime story. This entire plotline is out of place, but somehow Johansson makes it work. She earns our empathy through a realistic portrayal of a woman who is more of a fighter than we anticipate. Her resolve is as strong as her over-the-top Noo Yawk accent. 
 Though he dresses in sharp suits that would be at home in a scene from “American Psycho,” Driver plays Gary as a charismatic charmer rather than a sociopath with an ulterior motive. He’s a riveting study in contrasts. You know he’s bad news from his first scene, but there’s still a sense of brotherly love flowing from him. 
 Gary’s intentions aren’t meant to be harmful, but he underestimates his brother’s inexperience with bigshots and shady deals. Whether his actions in the final moments of the film are noble or self-serving, Gray leaves you to decide. 
 Adam Driver in “Paper Tiger.” NEON Driver’s performance is the fire burning under “Paper Tiger,” but it’s Teller who holds the film together. An actor I have never warmed to, Teller stunned me with the complexity he brought to Irwin. Gray wisely doesn’t make him a superhero or an angel of vengeance. Irwin earns our attention and empathy by being an Everyman trapped in the type of extenuating circumstances you can only find in a good crime noir. 
 A major step up from Gray’s last feature, the abysmal “ Armageddon Time ,” “Paper Tiger” is a flawed but effective thriller. 
 ★★★ 
 PAPER TIGER 
 Written and directed by James Gray. Starring Miles Teller, Scarlett Johansson, Adam Driver, Roman Engel, Gavin Goudey. At Coolidge Corner, AMC Boston Common. 115 min. R (this tiger’s tale is violent and profane) 
 Odie Henderson is the Boston Globe's film critic.
